summary: PRAXIS makes an agent 'practise' on a repository before real tasks: it re-implements selected existing functions (body removed, LLM-written description and test inputs) and is corrected by differential testing against the real implementation. What it got wrong is distilled into short knowledge units (trigger, content, evidence, confidence), anchored to functions on a call/data dependency graph and propagated to neighbours. These units are injected proactively, caller-side rules at task start and unit text appended to search/read/edit tool results. On the authors' own KoCo-Bench (about 131 Python tasks, one greedy run) with DeepSeek-V3.2 in OpenHands it solves 32.1% vs 27.5% for the best baseline (about 42 vs 36 tasks). Gains also appear with SWE-Agent and GPT-5.5, are tiny on Qwen3.6-Plus, and are modest on AInsteinBench bug fixing (27.2 -> 31.2%).

claims.claim: PRAXIS outperforms agentic-search agents and experience/skill-evolution methods (Pass@1 +16.7% relative over the best baseline)
claims.evidence: Table I: 32.06 vs 27.48 (OpenCollab, the authors' own earlier system) and 25.19 (Trace2Skill), i.e. about 42 vs 36 vs 33 of 131 tasks, one greedy run. A paired t-test (p<0.05) is reported for AvgPassRatio only. SWE-Exp falls below the raw base model (7.83 vs 10.69), suggesting a weak reimplementation, and one cell (SWE-Exp RL 6.15) is not a multiple of 1/53. The benchmark is from the same group.

claims.claim: Tacit knowledge is not recoverable by reading code; practice-based extraction is required
claims.evidence: Table II: replacing practice with direct extraction from source drops Pass@1 32.06 -> 27.48 (6 of 131 tasks, about one binomial SE, single run). Fig. 1 preliminary: giving all ground-truth dependency code +19.9% relative, adding agent-written exploration summaries only +4.8% relative more.

claims.claim: Graph organization, the structured unit format and proactive injection each contribute
claims.evidence: Table II: w/o graph 28.25, w/o procedural memory 29.01, w/o proactive injection (replaced by embedding retrieval) 28.24, vs 32.06. Each is 4-5 tasks of 131, from a single run with no significance test. 'w/o graph' removes propagation, deduplication and conflict resolution together.

claims.claim: Gains generalize across agent frameworks, LLMs and benchmarks, and scale with practice
claims.evidence: Table III: GPT-5.5 16.03 -> 42.75 (its baseline is oddly below DeepSeek's), SWE-Agent/DeepSeek 25.96 -> 35.12, Qwen3.6-Plus 25.95 -> 27.48 (2 tasks). Table IV: AInsteinBench 27.2 -> 31.2 with task counts not given. Scaling (1-10 practised functions) and online evolution appear only in figures; the RAG domain is flat.

claims.claim: Missing tacit knowledge is the root cause of domain-code failures, and the extracted units are high quality
claims.evidence: Root cause rests on manual failure analysis with no counts and one illustrated case (§II-B). Quality: two volunteer engineers rate 75 sampled units (truthfulness 4.28/5, evidence traceability 3.62/5), with no inter-rater agreement. LLM confidence correlates with human rating rho=0.75; 82% of 50 inspected trajectories use the knowledge.

patterns.note: Comparison: practice-based discovery (the agent re-implements existing functions under differential testing) vs reading-based discovery (direct extraction from source; agent exploration summaries). Practice wins 32.06 vs 27.48 Pass@1 (Table II), and summaries add only +4.8% relative over raw dependency code (Fig. 1). Margins are about 1 binomial SE on 131 tasks, single greedy run, one model for the ablation, authors' own benchmark. This is offline agent-side discovery, not human pre-spec discovery.
Structured units (trigger/content/evidence/confidence) vs flat text descriptions: 32.06 vs 29.01 (4 of 131 tasks, single run), within noise.

Anchoring knowledge to dependency-graph nodes with bidirectional propagation vs no graph organization: 32.06 vs 28.25. The ablation confounds propagation, deduplication and conflict resolution. Single-repo graph; no cross-repo edges.
Embedding retrieval of the same knowledge units scores 28.24 vs 32.06 for proactive entity-triggered injection, but still far above plain OpenHands (19.08). Delivery-mode effect is within noise.

A persistent knowledge base vs experience memory (SWE-Exp) and skill memory (Trace2Skill) on the same framework and model: 32.06 vs 7.83 and 25.19. SWE-Exp below the base model suggests a weak reimplementation. Trace2Skill is the fair comparator (about 9 tasks gap).

Read-only codebase exploration is not enough here. Agents with full repo access and agentic search (OpenHands, SWE-Agent, OpenCode, OpenCollab) solve 19-27%; agent-written exploration summaries add +4.8% relative; and the illustrated trajectory never seeks the missing cross-module contracts. Exploration grounded in execution feedback (practice) does better.

Property 3: the agent does not recognize its own tacit-knowledge deficit and never asks for or searches for it (one illustrated trajectory). This implies an ask-when-uncertain policy would not fire for tacit gaps. Not measured.
Differential testing against existing implementations is the signal that exposes knowledge during practice. It is not separated from the practice ablation.
The skill-distillation baseline (Trace2Skill) loses to entity-anchored injection, but it was re-run by the authors.

methodology.sample: KoCo-Bench: about 131 code-generation tasks (RL 53, Agent 52, Model Optimization 18, RAG 8; inferred from Pass@1 granularity) across 25 projects and 11 frameworks. AInsteinBench bug-fix tasks from 6 scientific codebases (count not given)
methodology.baselines: Base model; OpenHands, SWE-Agent, OpenCode, OpenCollab (the authors' earlier Self-collaboration); SWE-Exp and Trace2Skill re-run on the same framework. No Claude Code or Codex (which the authors call strongest) and no human-written AGENTS.md/docs baseline
methodology.models: DeepSeek-V3.2 (main), GPT-5.5, Qwen3.6-Plus; OpenHands and SWE-Agent frameworks
methodology.variance: Single greedy run at temperature 0; paired t-test p<0.05 on AvgPassRatio vs baselines only; nothing for Pass@1, ablations or cross-model results
methodology.ablations: Four single-component removals/replacements; scaling over 1-10 practised functions; online evolution
methodology.contamination_controls: Footnote says offline stages exclude evaluation test-set code. It does not say how target bodies are kept out of the practice repository and out of caller-anchored knowledge. KoCo-Bench was built by the same group
methodology.languages: Python (KoCo-Bench); AInsteinBench codebases include C++ (AMReX) and C/Fortran (Einstein Toolkit) alongside Python

biases.detail: Main benchmark (KoCo-Bench) authored by the same first author and group; one baseline (OpenCollab) is their earlier system.
Single greedy run; headline and ablation gaps are 4-6 of 131 tasks, about one binomial standard error.
SWE-Exp re-implementation scores below the raw model; strongest commercial agents omitted.
KoCo-Bench is Python; transfer to statically typed, framework-heavy Java untested.
131 tasks overall; the RAG domain has 8 tasks (one task = 12.5 pp). Human quality check is 75 units rated by 2 volunteers.
Practice uses ground-truth implementations of repository functions; isolation of evaluation targets from practice and caller-anchored knowledge is asserted, not described.
Offline practice cost per repository shown only in a figure; no tokens or dollars tabulated.
'Fundamental bottleneck', 'steady scaling' and 'consistent improvements' for 1-10 practised functions and a +2-task Qwen result.

coi.affiliations: Peking University (Key Lab of High Confidence Software Technologies); National University of Singapore; Shanghai Jiao Tong University
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: none commercial; the authors' own KoCo-Bench and OpenCollab/Self-collaboration
coi.detail: Benchmark authors ship the top-ranked system on their own benchmark; no commercial interest.

verdict_reason: A real mechanism with an informative ablation (practice beats reading) and repeated direction across frameworks, models and a second benchmark. But it is a single greedy run on the authors' own benchmark with margins of about one standard error, a weak experience-memory baseline, and contamination isolation that is asserted rather than described. Treat the effect sizes as optimistic.
applicability: Directly relevant to discovery and onboarding for undocumented ingestion conventions across 4+ Spring Boot repos. (1) Mine tacit contracts by having an agent re-implement existing service methods against JUnit tests or recorded-input differential checks, and store what it got wrong as short, entity-anchored rules (trigger, constraint, evidence link to the source method or diff, confidence). (2) Deliver rules where work happens: attach the rules for a class and its callers when an agent, or a newcomer's code-QA agent, opens or edits it, instead of relying on anyone to search. The paper shows the agent never realized it was missing a cross-module obligation, the 'register with the shared router' type of failure that bites the pipelines. (3) Do not expect read-and-summarize codebase tours to surface these; they added little here. Caveats: Python only, single repo (no cross-repo graph), and Java differential testing needs deterministic harnesses. Whether the same units help human developers onboard is untested, though they are human-readable and could seed review checklists.

conflicts_with.detail: That ablation finds no detectable correctness effect from how repository context (AGENTS.md) is delivered (none vs always-on vs on-demand) on 3 Python repos. PRAXIS reports about 4 pp from proactive vs embedding-retrieved delivery of mined knowledge. The content differs (mined contracts vs general instructions) and both are near noise, but they disagree on whether delivery mode matters.
